cards.b: The Sultanate (1206 to 1526) brought new administration, architecture and an urban economy. UPSC asks for rulers’ reforms and their effects.

• Slave (Mamluk) 1206 to 90: Qutbuddin Aibak, Iltutmish, Raziya, Balban.
  • Khalji 1290 to 1320: Jalaluddin, Alauddin.
  • Tughlaq 1320 to 1414: Ghiyasuddin, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firoz Shah.
  • Sayyid 1414 to 51; Lodi 1451 to 1526: Bahlol, Sikandar, Ibrahim Lodi.
The Sultanate ended with the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

Iltutmish (1211 to 36): got investiture from the Caliph, introduced the silver tanka and copper jital, the iqta system and the “Corps of Forty” (Turkan-i-Chahalgani); Qutb Minar finished. Raziya (1236 to 40): the only woman ruler. Balban (1266 to 87): divine kingship, sijda and paibos, strong spy system (barids), crushed the Forty and the Mongols; his court culture was Persian.

Conquests: Gujarat, Ranthambhor, Chittor, Malwa, and the south under Malik Kafur (Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra, Madurai). Mongol attacks repelled. Market reforms: price controls on grain, cloth, horses, with diwan-i-riyasat and shahna-i-mandi; to fund a large standing army. Land revenue at half the produce, measured (masahat) and direct (khalisa) collection; dagh (branding horses) and chehra (muster roll). Chroniclers: Amir Khusrau, Ziauddin Barani.

Famous “experiments”: (1) capital shift from Delhi to Daulatabad (1327, 1329 return); (2) token currency of brass and copper, which failed because of forgery; (3) taxation increase in the Doab and a famine; (4) the Khurasan and Qarachil plans; (5) agriculture department (diwan-i-kohi). Ibn Battuta (Moroccan, visited 1333 to 47) served as a judge. Rebellions began: Bahmani state (1347) and Vijayanagara (1336).

A reformer: new canals (Yamuna to Hisar), towns (Firozabad, Jaunpur, Fatehabad), the tax on Brahmins (jizya on them too), end of harsh punishments, slave department (diwan-i-bandagan), diwan-i-khairat (charity for marriages), and hereditary iqtas. Weak army; fall after his death. Timur’s invasion of Delhi (1398) shattered the Sultanate under Mahmud Tughlaq.

Sultan with the naib and wazir; departments: diwan-i-wizarat (finance), diwan-i-arz (army), diwan-i-insha, diwan-i-risalat. Provinces (iqta, later shiq), then parganas. Revenue: kharaj, jizya, zakat, khams. A money economy grew; Persian wheel, paper, spinning wheel and new crafts arrived. Cities such as Delhi, Multan and Lahore grew. Sultanate’s Hindu allies and Hindu elites served as revenue collectors.

cards.h: Was the Sultanate an Islamic state?
cards.b: Barani saw the state as divinely ordered; the Ulama pressed for sharia. Historians (Mohammad Habib, K. A. Nizami) show that rulers used both Persian kingship and local practice. Irfan Habib stressed the agrarian system and exploitation. Recent writers (Sunil Kumar) highlight a hybrid court. Alauddin’s remark that he ruled by what he thought best for the state is often quoted.

The Qutb complex, Tughlaqabad, and the Alai Darwaza are heritage sites. The idea of a standardised currency, price control (essential commodities act echoes), and the use of Persian in administration shaped later states. Debates on how to teach this period feed the NCERT and public memory debate.

• “Assess Alauddin Khalji’s market reforms.”
  • “Was Muhammad bin Tughlaq a mad king or a visionary?”
  • “Why did the Sultanate decline?”
  • Prelims tip: Iltutmish (iqta, tanka), Balban (sijda), Alauddin (market control, dagh), Tughlaq (token currency), Firoz (canals, diwan-i-khairat), Timur 1398.
